results.summary: Asicle v2 is a hardware implementation of the Wordle word-guessing game, rewritten for Tiny Tapeout after an earlier version on the Google-Skywater shuttle. It uses a QSPI Pmod for external flash to store the word list and font bitmaps, a Tiny VGA Pmod for video output, and a Gamepad Pmod or direct input pins for controls. The design runs at 25.175 MHz and requires flashing a data file to the QSPI Pmod before play. It is notable for fitting a complete game into a 2x2 tile area by moving data off-chip, and for its detailed documentation and debug features.

SimProc is an 8-bit processor that can be programmed and read back via UART using 3-byte packets. It has a UART receive input, a UART transmit output, and flags for halt and done. The baud rate is set by driving the bidirectional pins UIO7-UIO0. External hardware needed is a USB-to-UART converter or any UART device. The documentation is brief but sufficient to understand the basic operation.

This project is an instrumented ring oscillator with a selectable number of stages and a configurable initial state, intended for studying high-frequency modes rather than as a reliable clock source. It provides 16 phase outputs and uses a shift-register-like interface to seed the oscillator state. The design is controlled via input pins for enable, hold, stage selection, and seed data. Silicon tests confirmed functionality, though the slowest configuration runs near 50 MHz, requiring a spectrum analyzer and H-field probe for verification.

The QEI (Quadrature Encoder Interface) decodes A/B quadrature signals into a 15-bit up/down count and a direction flag. It synchronizes the inputs to the clock and outputs the count across the output and bidirectional pins. The design can be tested with an encoder connected directly for single-ended signals or via an RS-422 receiver for differential signals. It is a compact, straightforward implementation with clear documentation.

JulkeGussinatorn 2.0 is a Morse code entry and encryption/decryption device implemented in VHDL. Users input short and long Morse signals via buttons, lock in letters, and can encrypt or decrypt the stored message. An LED output displays the Morse code saved on the device. The documentation is minimal and the description is terse, but the basic functionality is clear from the pin names and text.

LEDs Racer is a multiplayer game where up to four players press arcade buttons to race their LED segment toward a center circle on a WS2812B LED ring. The design drives the LED data line and provides per-player ready-to-play indicators and a frame update signal. It requires external arcade buttons with pull-down resistors and a WS2812B LED ring. The documentation is brief but sufficient to understand the game and its hardware needs.

KianV uLinux RISC-V regfile edition is a 32-bit RISC-V IMA processor capable of booting Linux, featuring a 32x32 register file macro. It includes external SPI flash and PSRAM interfaces, a UART, and a SPI peripheral. The system runs at 30 MHz and requires a QSPI Pmod for external memory. Silicon tests showed partial functionality: it could not boot Linux due to an impedance mismatch when integrating the register file, though the register file itself works.

ASAP CPU v1 is a minimal SAP-1 inspired CPU with an 8-bit data path and 4-bit address space, running a built-in Fibonacci program. It outputs the current value in BCD to a multiplexed 7-segment display and provides a heartbeat signal. The design requires three common-cathode 7-segment displays and current-limiting resistors. It is an educational project influenced by Ben Eater and others, with clear documentation.

lime_cic_filter implements first-order and second-order Cascaded Integrator-Comb (CIC) filters for processing sigma-delta modulator bitstreams. It provides 16-bit output and includes debug selection inputs. The design requires no external hardware and is intended for digital signal processing applications. The documentation is partly AI-generated and lacks a detailed test plan, but the core functionality is described.

VGA Pattern Generator produces colorful geometric patterns on a VGA monitor at 640x480 @ 60 Hz. It uses a 25 MHz pixel clock and generates patterns procedurally from pixel coordinates, with input switches selecting between modes and palettes. The design requires a TinyVGA PMOD adapter and a VGA monitor. Silicon tests confirmed working patterns that change with input toggles.
